title: Pulp exposures secondary to trauma can be amenable to conservative pulp therapies which conserve vital pulp tissue which can allow for continued root development.
Pulp exposure during caries excavation in which bleeding cannot be controlled is a strong indicator of irreversible pulpitis.
Endodontic disease/apical periodontitis is mainly caused by:
Apical periodontitis is an inflammatory response to an infective process caused by bacteria.

32 year old patient presents with a chief complaint that includes spontaneous and lingering pain to cold fluids. Upon radiographic exam you notice decay approximating the pulp of tooth #3. After caries excavation you notice there is no pulpal exposure. This is a strong indicator that a root canal can be avoided and that all that is needed is a well-sealed restoration.

Patient presents with a chief complaint of pain around his lower anterior teeth. He is not sure which tooth specifically is causing the discomfort. Upon radiographic examination you notice a significant periapical lesion that spans the apex of teeth #23, 24, 25. Because the lesion is touching the roots of these three teeth it is a strong indicator that all three teeth will require root canal therapy.

A patient with an acute apical abscess associated with a necrotic pulp should be treated with a root canal. If the patient calls the day after you start the root canal and tells you the swelling is getting worse you should then tell the patient to only take an antibiotic if they develop fever.
A sinus tract exiting on the gingiva adjacent to tooth #30 is an indication that tooth #30 is definitely the tooth that is causing the chronic apical abscess.
A tooth with a chronic apical abscess is usually quite sensitive to percussion.
There is never a justification to doing a root canal on a tooth with a healthy pulp.

Patient presents with decay on tooth #30. Radiographic exam reveals an open apex on both the mesial and distal roots. Upon caries excavation the pulp is exposed. The exposure measures 3 mm in diameter. After bleeding is controlled, you remove 2-3 of the coronal pulp tissue and place a bio-cermic material directly on the pulp. The term that best fits this procedure is:
final: Indirect pulp cap
